chunks: "Series termination puts a resistor at the driver so that driver plus resistor equals the line impedance.

The line sees half the swing, the wave goes down the line, hits the open end of the receiver, doubles to full swing, and the reflection travels back and is absorbed at the source, so there's no ringing.
It uses essentially no DC power, it's one small resistor, and the driver only sees the AC load.

The downside is that the signal only reaches full amplitude after the reflection returns, so it only works with receivers at the end of the line: anything tapped off the middle sees a half-amplitude shelf, and the edge is a bit slower.
Parallel termination puts a resistor equal to Z 0 at the receiver, to ground or to a bias voltage.
The wave is absorbed on arrival with no reflection at all, so every receiver along the way sees a full, clean edge. That's best for multi-drop buses and the fastest links.
The costs: DC power, since a 3.
3 volts signal into 50 ohms to ground burns about 200 milliwatts whenever it's high; a reduced high level because of the divider with the driver; and the driver has to supply the current.
So: point-to-point, low power, moderate speed, I'd use series.
Multi-drop, bidirectional or very fast, and power isn't a constraint, I'd use parallel, usually as Thevenin, AC or on-die termination."
